title: The Longshots
full_review:
The fictional Midwestern city that provides the setting for the fact-based sports drama "The Longshots" (Dimension/MGM) is beset by a number of all-too-familiar problems. Its factory is closed, its main street is decaying and even the once-mighty local football team, the Minden Browns -- part of the nationwide Pop Warner youth league -- has suffered two decades of decline.

A typical victim of these depressed conditions is Curtis Plummer (Ice Cube, also a producer). Once a high school gridiron star, he's now unemployed and unkempt and spends his days drinking beer while nurturing his dream of relocating to Miami. First as a favor, but in the end as a part-time job, his hardworking sister-in-law, Claire (Tasha Smith), asks him to mind Jasmine (Keke Palmer), his shy, bookish niece.

 

An outsider at school, Jasmine has never recovered from the fact her irresponsible father, Roy (Malcolm Goodwin), deserted her and she still wears his watch as a symbol of her hope to reconnect. She's unwilling to be watched by a baby sitter, especially an uncle for whom she has scant respect, and the two bicker constantly.

By chance, though, Curtis discovers that Jasmine has an excellent throwing arm. After giving her some rudimentary training, he sets out to convince the Browns' coach (Matt Craven) that awarding Jasmine the quarterback spot on his previously all-boys team will reverse their sliding fortunes.

As the heavily tattooed lead singer of the often-controversial band Limp Bizkit, director Fred Durst may seem an unlikely heir of Hollywood's most famous American dreamer, Frank Capra (1897-1991). Yet his upbeat, mostly unobjectionable film, which also features Garrett Morris as a dynamic preacher and community leader, is a Capraesque celebration of each individual's power to bring about both personal and civic renewal.

The film contains brief sexual humor, a couple of profanities, a few crass words and mild oaths. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.
